questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The availability of courses related to my field of studies. The new network, job, and academic opportunities are relations that the destination could offer for my future personal and professional carrier

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I rated 8, because of course the exchange experience was great and gave me the opportunity to dive into a new culture, create new relations, and meet many great and interesting people. But the process was very difficult to carry out, and i didn't receive any guidance both from home and host university. In addition, most of the courses that i applied to weren't open to exchange students and this was notified only when i already applied for my exchange so i couldn't change my priorities.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Not very easy, as we were told to have an orientation week (during the first week of august), but that was never held - so it make it very challenging to find all the information ie: finding classrooms, getting your way around campus, understanding how everything works.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: emails from host university. some events, but very difficult to get a spot as we were a lot of exchangers.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: the orientation week did not take place

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: finding housing off-campus in Singapore is very difficult and can get very expensive. there are some websites that can put you in contact with private hosts, or private dorms (that can provide a cheap option). Facebook groups work quite well and asking around if you have any contact in Singapore. I was lucky enough to find housing through a private host.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Shared houses in Singapore are not very common thing. And you don't spend a lot of time at home so even just one room is fine. Don't be scared off by the no cooking/ only light cooking rule (which may be there in some houses or dorms) - in Singapore, you mainly eat out ( also because the cheapest and most convenient option) so you won't find yourself cooking much.

How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Registration was pretty straightforward, but if you are a master's student keep in mind that there are very few courses available. But keep in mind that if you are not assigned the courses you want right away, you can change them with late registration.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: A list of courses open to exchange students is available. You can choose a minimum of 3 courses up to a maximum of 5. The 1000 to 4000 levels are bachelor's and the 5000 level is master's. You apply on the portal and for most courses you need to fill out a form to prove you are eligible for the course.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: course registration guide. and ask for help from other students.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was able to secure two courses I wanted ( out of 3) and for one I had to compromise. But I had to go through the registrar's office several times to secure master's level courses.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Look at the list of courses open for exchange students in advance, before applying to the host university. For master students, NUS is not ideal as the courses at the master level are not available, and you have to compromise with some undergrad courses.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: courses were mostly interesting, a very different approach form KU.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level of the courses was similar to KU, but the approach is very different. NUS use mostly continuous assessment as a way of assessing student, so you have a lot of hand-in, paper, and quizzes to carry out throughout the course - that can be challenging at first if you are not used to that.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: NUS use mostly continuous assessment as a way of assessing student, so you have a lot of hand-in, paper, and quizzes to carry out throughout the course - that can be challenging at first if you are not used to that.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Majorities and minorities in SE Asia (BA)
Food product development and packaging (BA)
Global Food Policy and Sustainable Food System (MA)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Majorities and minorities in SE Asia (BA) --> I would recommend this course if you want to have a better overview of SE Asia's culture and political situation. Is a seminar base course, meaning that the lecture is very brief and most of the class is a discussion on the readings you have to prepare at home

Food product development and packaging (BA) --> I would recommend this course to undergrad students in food science as is a very nice hands-on course, where you get to develop a food product and packaging in collaboration start-up from scratch. (Include lab practice)

Global Food Policy and Sustainable Food System (MA) I would recommend this course to master students interested in food policies and research methods in the field of food systems. Very nice course the one that was most related to my studies.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The people i've met and the network that it allowed me to create. and the travels opportunities

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Adjust to the commuting lifestyle of a metropolis like Singapore, at least 2 hours of subway rides per day :)))

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: a bit challenging with the bureaucratic issues (application, course registration, visa), but DEFINITELY worth it! I would recommend it to anyone
